sentences.text: The genus Limnofregata was established by Olson in 1977 and belongs to the family Fregatidae.
The type species, Limnofregata azygosternon, is known from numerous complete and partial skeletons, some preserving feather impressions.
These birds resembled modern frigatebirds but possessed shorter, less-hooked bills, longer legs, and longer slit-like nasal openings.
They stood 30 to 40 cm tall on the ground and had a wingspan of approximately 100 to 120 cm.
The throat bones of Limnofregata differ markedly from those of modern frigatebirds.
The first two species were described based on fossils found in the Early Eocene Green River Formation of Wyoming, dating to approximately 49 million years ago.
The species differ significantly in size, with L. hasegawai being much larger than L. azygosternon, similar to the size difference between the largest and smallest modern frigatebird species.
Unlike their modern marine relatives, Limnofregata fossils were recovered from prehistoric freshwater environments.
Researchers suggest Limnofregata lived like gulls of the genus Larus, a behavior supported by their longer legs adapted for swimming.
They likely fed on smaller vertebrates, harassed other shorebirds for food, and scavenged dead fish like Knightia during summer oxygen-depletion events in eutrophic lakes.
Because Limnofregata was likely not a soaring bird, researchers expect that males and females were similar in size.
The third species, L. hutchisoni, is at least 53 million years old, and possibly as old as 54 or 55 million years.
The genus lived during the Ypresian stage, from 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
Fossil beds containing crocodiles, large trionychid turtles, and fish indicate that Limnofregata lived in a sizeable body of water.
